title: Two clinics, one hospital, very different odds. In Vienna the doctors' clinic lost about 10% of
description:
In Vienna the doctors' clinic lost about 10% of mothers to childbed fever. The midwives' clinic lost under 4%. Those are average rates for 1841 to 1846 at the Vienna General Hospital.

Semmelweis's colleague. He died after a student's scalpel cut him during a post mortem, and his autopsy resembled those of the women.

Mortality was 18.3% in April 1847. After handwashing in chlorinated lime began, June was 2.2%. Doctors had been going from the autopsy room straight to the delivery ward without cleaning their hands.

Roughly how far deaths in the First Clinic fell once handwashing began.

Most contemporaries rejected the idea, and Rudolf Virchow was among them. He had no theory to explain it, and germ theory had not yet taken hold in Vienna.

He died in 1865, aged 47, of a septic wound.

Sources:
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ignaz_Semmelweis: read in full. Established that in the Vienna General Hospital the First Clinic averaged about 10% maternal mortality from puerperal fever against under 4% in the Second Clinic, that colleague Jakob Kolletschka died after a scalpel cut during a post mortem and his autopsy resembled the women's, that Semmelweis introduced chlorinated lime handwashing in 1847, that mortality was 18.3% in April 1847 and 2.2% in June after handwashing began in mid May, that First Clinic mortality fell by about 90%, that Rudolf Virchow was among those who rejected his ideas, and that he died on 13 August 1865 aged 47 with pyemia listed as the cause.
- https://www.sciencealert.com/ignaz-semmelweis: read in full. Independently established that doctors' ward mothers had roughly a one in 10 chance of dying against about half that risk with midwives, that Kolletschka died in 1847 from an infected post mortem wound, that mortality fell from around 18 percent in April 1847 to less than 2 percent by July, that senior staff resisted, and that Semmelweis died on 13 August 1865 from an infected hand wound.
